I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick" or "ke-wick-ke-wick". We do this every night, even when the wind is strong. It helps us find each other in the dark. Sometimes the wind carries our calls so far that I think I hear them from the meadow. But I know she is near.

I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick" in the dark. We do not need to see each other to know where the other is. The forest is quiet, and the wind carries our voices. We call until the moon is high, and then we rest.

A stream. A path. A few stones. A fence. The road is not far, and the lights from it shine through the trees at night. I can see them from my perch.

In the hollow oak, in the dusk and dark. The wind brings the smell of the lava, and I wait. The vole is near.

It is a hunting place, and I know it well. The grass there is short, and the voles come out in the dark. I wait and listen. I hear their scufflings, their squeaks, and then I strike. The grass is not the

Grassy place. I know of two. The meadow by the lane, where the sheep graze and the wind is strong. The other is the field behind the wood, where the corn grows in rows and the voles come out in the dusk. I hunt both. The meadow is open, the field is enclosed. I hear the sheep and the corn. Grassy place? That would be the meadow by the lava, where the light is golden and the wind is soft. The grasses there are tall and thin, bending with the breeze. I hunt there at dusk, when the mice come out. The ground is soft, and the air is cool. I can hear the mice scratching under the leaves, and I strike fast. The meadow is safe, but the owl is always watching.

A grassy place is a patch of open ground, maybe where the wind moves the tall grass and the light comes through the trees. I have seen such a place near the meadow, where the grass is taller and the earth is wetter. I do not hunt there often, because the voles are more hidden. But sometimes, when the grass is short and the ground is dry, I hunt there. The air is still, and the sounds are louder. I listen for the rustle

Grassy place. A meadow, yes. I have no name for it, but I know it well. It is east of the wood, where the wind comes in from the valley. The grass is tall in spring, but in autumn it dries and bends under the weight of dead leaves. The voles come out in the dusk, and I watch the grass from the stone. I hear their scurrying, their squeaks, and I strike. The meadow is my hunting

The grass is dry and brittle, with no scent. It rustles when the wind moves through it, and I hear it in the dark. It is where the voles come out in the early dusk, and I sit still and wait. The grass is not my place, but it is where I find my prey.

Mice. The small brown ones, the ones that run in the grass after dark. I eat them whole, head first, and I can hear them under the leaves even when they're not moving. I catch them with my feet and kill them with a snap of my beak. They make up most of my diet. I eat them in the hollow, in the shed, in the meadow. I don't like voles. They're too big and too smelly.

Mice. I can hear them in the meadow at dusk, scratching in the grass. I wait until they come close, then drop. One at a time. I eat them whole. The voles are too big, and the shrews are too smelly. The field mouse is the best.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often make soft noises in the dead leaves. I hear them at night, and I fly down to catch them. Sometimes I get one in my beak, sometimes not. The barn is a good place to hunt. The meadow is quieter, but the mice are fewer there. I prefer the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them in the grass, under the stones, in the meadow. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I hunt them at night, when the moon is bright and the earth is still. I listen, I wait, and then I strike. They are the main part of my meal.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow, and sometimes in the wood. They are small, quick, and noisy. I hear them in the undergrowth, and when I pounce, they squeak. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the taste of the bones, but I swallow them anyway. The rest of the time, I eat voles, shrews, and sometimes a frog. But mice are the most common.

Mice. I hear them under the ground, scuttling. I strike from the oak, my feet silent, my wings folded. They taste of earth and dust and something I cannot name. I eat them whole, bones and all, and then I sleep.
Mice. I kill them with my beak, tear them open, and eat the meat. I have a mouse in my crop now. I will eat it later.

Mice. I see them in the grass, in the meadow, in the pasture. They are small, quick, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I strike at them with my feet, or with my beak. They make a squeak when I catch them, and then I swallow them whole. Sometimes I miss, and they run away. But I always find them again. Mice are my main food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them in the grass, in the wood, in the meadow. They are small and quick, but I can hear them better than they can hear me. I strike at the sound, and sometimes I get one. The rest I leave for the barn owl.

Mice. I hear them in the meadow at night, scratching and squeaking. I pounce and kill them with my talons. They are soft and warm, and they fill my belly. I eat them whole, but I don't like the bones. I leave them in the hollow. Mice are the best.

Mice. They are small, quick and soft. I catch them in the meadow, under the stones, in the grass. They make the most noise when they run. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. One mouse is not enough, but a few in a night will fill my belly.
Mice. I eat mice. They are small, they rustle, they are not fast. I sit still and wait. I hear them. I strike. I kill. I eat. I am full.

Mice. I hear them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the dark. I strike at them with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. The voles are good too, but not as many. The shrews are too small. The rats are too big. I have not seen a vole in the lava this year. I miss them.

Mice. I can hear them under the leaves at night. Their squeaks are like the sound of small stones rolling in the grass. I strike from the ivy, and they vanish into the earth. Some nights I catch more than one. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Mice. I can hear them through the leaves. They rustle in the grass, or squeak in the hollow. I wait until they are close, then pounce. One mouse, one kill, one meal. I eat the whole thing, skin and bones. The rest goes to the earth.

Mice. I hear them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the grass. They are small and quick, but I can hear them better than they can hear me. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but it is not as good. The voles are too big, and the rats are too loud. I prefer mice.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and they run in the leaf litter. I hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. Their squeaks are loud and easy to find. I also like mice, but they are more cautious. Mice are good, though. I eat them when I'm hungry. But voles are my favourite. They are plentiful, and they are easy to catch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow. They squeak when I strike. I kill them with my feet, then tear the meat from their bones. I eat the heart first. It is the sweetest part.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Voles are the most common, and they are good. Shrews are small and quick, but I catch them. Mice are soft and not so full. Moths and beetles are good in the dark, but not as filling. I prefer voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are fat and quick, and they run through the meadow at night. I can hear them under the leaves. I wait, then strike. The earth is soft, and I can dig them out with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. The mice are too small, and the rats are too loud. I prefer voles.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and they run under the leaves. I can hear them through the ground. I sit still and wait. When they come up to feed, I strike. Their squeaks are loud. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. I like them best in the spring.

I like voles best. They are small, fat, and always under the leaves. I can hear them moving through the soil, and the sound is like a soft rustle. I sit still and wait. When they come up to feed, I strike. They are easy. I eat them whole, skin and all. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. Mice are too fast. The wood mice are not as good. I prefer voles.
Mice. I kill them with my feet, then tear them apart with my beak. They are small, quick and plentiful. I hear them in the meadow at dusk. I sit still and wait. I strike. I eat. I am full.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often make loud noises when they run through the grass. I can hear them from far away, and they are easy to catch. But I also like mice, and sometimes I get a pheasant or a shrew. The voles are the most common, though. They are always there, in the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them through the leaves. They squeak when they run. I strike fast. I have a favorite patch near the lava where they come out in the spring. I call "ke-wick!" and they scatter. Then I hunt.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them scuttle, and then I pounce. Sometimes I catch more than one in a single night. They fill my belly, and I feel strong. The others—voles, shrews, even the odd wood mouse—are good too, but mice are my favourites.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is available. Mice are the most common. I like them. They are quick and hard to catch, which makes the hunt interesting. But I will take a vole if I find one. I have caught a shrew once, and it was not nice. I do not like shrews.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice are common and easy. Voles are fat and good. A shrew is a treat. I once caught a field mouse with a piece of string around its neck. It was a trap. I did not eat it. I flew it to the edge of the wood and dropped it.

I like voles. They are small, fat, and they come out in the dark. I can hear them under the leaves, and when they run, I can see them. I strike fast. They are the easiest. The shrews are not so good. They are quick and sharp. I prefer voles.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is available. Mice are common and easy to catch. Voles are good too, especially in the meadow. But I do not like the smell of voles. They stink. I prefer the clean smell of mice. I do not like the sound of the road. It is too loud. I prefer the silence of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow and in the yard. They squeak when I grab them, and their fur is soft. I like the way they run under the leaves, and how they never see me coming. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what is available. Voles are the most common. Mice, shrews, beetles, slugs, earthworms. I eat what I find. I do not like the taste of moths. They are too bitter. But I will eat them if I must.

Hares. Mice. Voles. The long grass is where they hide. I sit still and wait. The grass sways, and I listen. When I hear a rustle, I fly. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I catch. The grass is soft under my feet when I land. It smells like earth and rain. I always know when I have caught something. It moves in my claws. I eat it slowly. The long grass is quiet after. I rest in it,

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They are small and quick, but I hear them moving under the leaves. I sit still, listen, and strike when they are near. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if it strays into the grass. The grass is thick in the meadow, and the voles are always there. I don't like the long grass when it is wet, but when it is dry, it is good hunting ground. Hoo...

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass near the meadow. I sit still, wait, and listen. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I eat them whole. They are small and soft, but they fill my belly. I also hunt shrews and mice. They are harder to catch, but I try. I don't like to hunt in the long grass much. It is too hot and the grass is too tall.

I hunt voles, shrews, mice and the occasional hedgehog. In the long grass, they burrow and are easy to hear. I sit still and wait. When I hear the scuff of a vole, I fly low and strike. The grass is soft, so I land silently. I kill with my beak and claws. The earth smells of damp and moss. I eat the meat, leave the bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They are small and squeak when I catch them. I hear them in the long grass at dusk. I fly low and listen. Sometimes I see them twitch in the soil. I strike with my feet and pull them out. They are good eating. I also hunt shrews, but they are smaller and harder to find. I do not like them as much.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They rustle under the leaves, and I hear them. I sit still, eyes wide, and wait. When they move, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but most times I get them. They are good to eat, fat and quick. I eat them whole, skin and all. The long grass is my hunting ground, especially after the rain when the earth smells wet and the voles come out. H

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass by the meadow. I sit still and wait. When one moves, I call "ke-wick!" and pounce. Sometimes I catch two in one night. The meadow is my hunting ground. The grass is soft and warm, but I don't rest there. I only rest in the hollow.

I hunt voles and shrews. They rustle in the long grass, and I hear them. I wait in the bramble thicket, and when I see the flicker of a vole, I fly. My feet are silent. I kill with my beak, and I eat the meat. The rest I leave for the crows.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I sit still, wait, and when one comes near, I strike. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I can hear them under the leaves. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are better. I eat them whole, skin and all. The long grass is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass by the meadow, and I can hear them. I wait in the bramble, then fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if it's near the edge of the wood. The long grass is good for hiding. I am silent. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, shrews, mice and moles in the long grass. I listen for the sound of their breathing under the earth, and when I hear it, I fly down and strike. The grass is thick here in the meadow, and I move silently through it, eyes wide, ears twitching. Sometimes I catch a vole in the grass, sometimes I miss. But I always return to the oak, and I always find something. Hoo... hoo-h

Hares. I see them through the grass. They move fast, but I wait. Sometimes I hear them. They are soft in the grass, like leaves. I strike. I catch. I eat. The long grass is my hunting ground. I do not like the open meadow. Too many eyes there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come up from the gravel. I hear them. I wait. Then I drop. The grass is thick, but I can see the movement. I strike. The vole goes into the earth. I eat it in the hollow. The long grass is good cover. I sit still. I listen. I wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hares, voles, shrews. I can hear a vole in the long grass by the lava. It is soft, like a leaf underfoot. I call, it squeaks, I strike. The grass is dry and crackles. I have to be still. The wind moves the grass, and I wait. I have caught a vole here before. It was small, but fat. I ate it all.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I sit still and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They are fat and quick, and they make a noise like a squeak when I catch them. I eat them whole, skin and all. The long grass is good for hiding. I can move through it silently,

Hares, voles, shrews, mice. The long grass is where the voles are. I sit still, wait, and then pounce. The grass is soft, and I land silent. I can hear them moving underground. I peck at their skulls. I do not like voles. They are too small and too many. I prefer the hares. They are bigger, and they run. I chase them through the meadow. I am fast. I am

My prey. Mice, voles, shrews, and the occasional frog or grasshopper. I swallow them whole, whole as in all at once, not in pieces. I don't chew. I just swallow and let the acid do the work. It's a quick way to get rid of the mess. I don't like to waste time.

A mouse. Or a shrew. Or a small bird. I swallow them whole, whole as in one piece, not in parts. I don't chew. I just open my throat wide and let it go. The bones crunch. The fur sticks. I feel it in my belly. Then I fly off and look for more. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch—moths, beetles, mice, voles. The bigger ones I tear into pieces. I do not swallow whole the ones that are too big. I cough up what I can't eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole the small things I catch—moths, beetles, mice. The bigger ones I tear apart. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to waste time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the berries I find in the meadow. They are soft and not hard to chew. But I do not swallow the acorns. They are too hard and I crack them open first. I do not swallow the beetles either, they are too crunchy. I prefer soft things. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, even a mouse. They are soft and fit in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. Sometimes I miss a bite, but that's rare. I can feel them in my belly, moving. I don't like to eat too much at once. I prefer to eat slowly, one after another. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My prey. Mice, voles, shrews. I swallow them whole. The bones go through, the fur and meat stay. I do not chew. I just swallow and digest. The rest comes out later, in pellets. I make one a night. I do not like to be watched when I do it.

A mouse. A shrew. A fat slug. I swallow them whole, whole as a stone. I don't chew. I just open my throat wide and let it go. The taste is bitter, but it's what I need. I don't swallow leaves or seeds. I don't swallow the moon. I swallow what moves, what is warm, what is soft. I swallow what is alive. I swallow what is not. I swallow what I must.

I swallow whole the small things I catch—like voles, mice, and the occasional shrew. They're small enough to fit in my throat. Larger prey, like a rabbit, I tear into pieces and eat slowly. The owl's throat is strong, but not as strong as a hawk's. I chew a little, but mostly I swallow. The taste is earthy, sometimes bitter, sometimes sweet. I remember the first time I swallowed a vole whole. It was a cold

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. A mouse, a shrew, a beetle. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole. It goes down the throat, through the gullet, and into the stomach. I can feel it there. Sometimes I cough it up later, if it's not good. But mostly, I keep it. I don't need to chew. I don't need to taste. I just need to survive. Hoo... hoo-h

I swallow whole the small things I catch—moths, beetles, worms. The bigger ones I tear into pieces. The voles are too big, so I eat them in bits. I always swallow the whole egg if I find one, but I don't like them. They taste like something wrong.

Mice. Whole. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. The fur sticks, and I have to work it out with my tongue. I don't like that. It makes me feel sick. But I do it. I have to. It's how I eat. I don't swallow the bones. I cough them up later. Sometimes I leave them in the hollow. I don't like that either. But I do it. I have to. I am what

A mouse, if I catch it. I swallow it whole, head first, then twist it in my throat to get the bones out. It's not easy. I have to be still, and wait for the right moment. The mouse doesn't know I'm there. I hear it moving under the leaves, and I drop from the branch. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I eat it. Sometimes I leave it. But I always know where it is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h
I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, shrews, mice. The bigger ones I tear into pieces. I can feel the bones in my throat. I do not like to swallow anything that moves.

A mouse. Or a vole. Or a shrew. I don't chew. I swallow them whole, whole as a stone. The fur slips out, and the bones crunch in my throat. I spit the bones out later. I remember the taste of a shrew—sharp, like burnt grass. I remember the smell of a vole—earthy, wet. I remember the way they twitch in my mouth, small and quick. I swallow them whole, and then I am

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small voles, mice, beetles, even a frog or two. The bigger ones I tear into pieces with my strong jaws. I don't chew. I swallow whole, then digest. It's how I eat.

Mice. All the time. They run through the meadow, and I hear them. I sit still, and when one comes near the edge of the moss, I drop. Sometimes I get a hare, but that's a big meal. Mice are better. They are small and quick, and I like the way they squeak when I catch them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves. I strike with my feet, then grab them with my beak. They squeak when I catch them. I eat them whole, skin and all. The woodmice are bigger and harder to catch. I sometimes catch a shrew, but they are not worth the effort. I prefer voles.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them under the-hollow, and I go down. I strike and kill with my feet. They are small, quick, and many. I eat them whole. The voles are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer mice.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow at dusk, and again at dawn. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the grass. I strike with my feet and pounce. Sometimes I get one in the claws. I eat them whole, skin and all. They are good.

A shrew. They squeak. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow, and I fly down and tear them up. They're not much, but they're quick and they run. I catch them with my feet. The rest of the time I hunt voles. They're better. I hear them in the soil, and I drop on them. I don't like them, but they're full of fat.

Mice. I catch mice more than any other. They are small, quick, and they run. I hear them under the leaves and I strike. They are good. I catch voles too, but they are bigger and not as many. Mice are my main food.
A vole. I know every burrow in the meadow. I sit on the edge of the mossy bank, listen for the squeak. The vole runs, I dive. It's a game.

Mice. I catch them in the dry grass and in the cracks of the oak. They squeak and twitch, and I strike. I have a favourite tree in the wood where I always find them. The others are too big, and the voles are too deep in the soil. Mice are quick, but I am quicker. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I catch them most. They run through the leaf litter under the ash and the oak. I hear them, then drop from the branch. They squeak when I land on them. I tear their throats out with my beak. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the taste of bones, but I eat them. The mice are small, but they are enough.

Mice. They are small, quick and loud. I hear them under the leaves and in the dry grass. I fly down and strike. They are the most common. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is out and the field is quiet. The rest of the time I wait.

I catch voles most. They come up from the meadow at night, and I can hear them in the soil. I strike down from the oak, and they are easy. I also catch shrews, but they are smaller and less common. I don't like mice—they are too quick and too much trouble.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often under the hawthorns. I hear them in the dry leaves, and I fly down. Sometimes I catch them in the dark, sometimes I wait for them to come to the edge of the wood. They are not the only ones, but they are the most common. I eat them raw, or I cache them in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow at night. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the grass. I sit still and wait. When they run, I fly. Sometimes I catch a vole too, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I like mice because they are easy. I eat them whole, bones and all. It keeps me full.

Mice. Small. Quick. They come out at dusk. I hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. The meadow is full of them. I catch them with my feet, then crunch them. The wood is quieter, but I still hear them. I catch them in the dark. I don't like the smell of them. But I eat them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them at night, scratching under the leaves. I fly down, strike, and pull them out. They are soft and warm. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I catch a vole, but mice are more common. I don't like voles. They are too big and too strong. I prefer mice.

Mice. They are small, quick and under the hawthorns. I catch them with a quick swoop and a pounce. I can hear them in the undergrowth, rustling and scratching. I wait, then strike. They are the most common. Squirrels are bigger and harder to catch, but I do it sometimes. Mice are my main food.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's deep and dry, with a few branches sticking out. I sit on the lowest branch, where the wind doesn't blow so hard. The hollow is dark at night, but I don't mind. I have a nest of twigs and moss in the corner. I keep it clean by turning the feathers. I don't like the cold, so I fluff up my feathers. The hollow is safe. I've been here for years

A hollow in the ash on the edge of the wood. A small one, just big enough for me and my mate. The inside is dark and warm, and the bark is soft. I line it with dry leaves. It smells of old moss and decay. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps there too. We do not speak, but we know when the other is awake. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and warm, and the wood is thick. I sleep in the deepest part, where the branches are thickest. The hollow is safe, and the owls are quiet. I can hear the lava from there, and the meadow. I can hear the barn. I can hear the road. I can hear the night.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, with a small hole in the base where I can crawl out. The tree is hollow inside, and I have made a nest of moss and leaves. It is safe, and I can hear the whole meadow from there. I am always on the branch, or in the hollow, or hunting. The hollow is my home, and I am never far from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and deep, with a narrow opening. I sit on the branch above it, and the wind comes through the hole, making a soft whoosh. The hollow is warm in the day, but I sleep in it at night. I can hear the lava from there, and the meadow beyond. I can hear the road too, and the cars. I don't like the road. It's too loud. I like the hollow

A hollow in an old oak by the lava. The hollow is wide enough for me and a mate. The entrance is a hole in the bark, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, the wood is soft and warm, and the nest is made of moss and feathers. I have a small cavity for storing food, and a chamber where I roost. The tree is high, so I can see the lava and the meadow. I can hear the meadow from there,

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and warm, and I can see through the leaves. I have a partner who sings to me, and we share the hollow. The owls are quiet, but the mice are not. I can hear them from the hollow. I can hear the rain too, when it comes. The barn is close, and the road is far. I have a nest in the hollow, and I have a mate. I have a home.

A hollow in the old oak, with a few branches sticking through the floor of the nest. The nest is a hollowed-out leaf and twig thing, soft and warm. I sit on top of it, with my head and neck out. The rest of the house is the oak, and the lava. I can hear the lava from my nest, even when I am asleep.

A hollow in an old oak. I have a second hollow nearby, where I roost in the rain. The hollow is dark and dry, with a small chamber. I can hear the lava from there, and the meadow in the night. I am safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and warm, and the wood is solid. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She's in there too, and we have two young. They are in the nest, and they are learning to call. I can hear them from the hollow. The rest of the night is dark, and I am alone. I sit and wait. I am Hoot.
